title: High API error rate
trigger: Any service reports HTTP 5xx above 5% for five consecutive minutes.
steps: Confirm the error rate against the service dashboard rather than the alert payload alone.
List deploys and config changes in the preceding 60 minutes for the service and its direct dependencies.
Read application logs for the first minute of the spike and record the dominant error class.
Check each direct dependency for its own alerts before assuming the fault is local.
Compare current error rate with the same window on the previous day to separate a regression from a traffic shift.
If a deploy lines up with the onset, follow RB-22 for the rollback decision.
Escalate to the owning team with the timeline if no candidate cause is identified within 20 minutes.

title: Payment API Redis dependency failure
trigger: payment-api reports Redis timeouts, pool checkout failures, or connection errors.
steps: Read the client-side pool metrics first: in-use connections, pool size, and checkout wait time per replica.
Separate app-side exhaustion from dependency-side saturation. Pool in-use equal to pool size with healthy Redis means app-side; Redis refusing connections means dependency-side.
Check redis-cache connected_clients against maxclients, and multiply the per-replica pool by the current replica count before changing either.
Check Redis server latency, evicted_keys, and memory before blaming the client.
Compare the current release against the previous one for new Redis calls per request.
Do not change pool size on the strength of a single past incident. INC-1042 raised it and INC-1198 had to reverse that. Aggregate utilisation decides which applies.
Escalate to platform if redis-cache itself is at a server-side limit.

title: Redis connection saturation
trigger: redis-cache reports 'max number of clients reached' or refuses new connections.
steps: Read connected_clients and maxclients from the Redis node and record the ratio.
Break connected_clients down by client name to find which service holds the most.
For the top consumer, compute replica count multiplied by per-replica pool size and compare it against maxclients.
Prefer reducing the oversized client pool over raising maxclients; raising the ceiling moves the limit to node memory.
Check whether a recent autoscaling event raised the replica count without a pool change.
Escalate to database on-call if the same pattern appears on pgbouncer.

title: Redis memory pressure and key eviction
trigger: redis-cache evicted_keys is rising or used_memory is near maxmemory.
steps: Read used_memory, maxmemory, and evicted_keys, and record the eviction rate per minute.
Read maxmemory-policy. Under allkeys-lru, keys without a TTL can also be evicted, including live sessions.
Identify the largest keyspaces with a sampled scan; do not run KEYS on the production node.
Check the cache hit rate of the affected service to confirm evictions and not a code change caused the misses.
Separate session data from cache data so a memory ceiling cannot drop live sessions.
Escalate to platform before raising maxmemory above the node's safe headroom.

title: Postgres unavailable or failover stalled
trigger: Postgres primary is unreachable, or a failover has not completed within the detection window.
steps: Confirm from two vantage points that the primary is genuinely unreachable and not just slow.
Read the Patroni cluster state and check whether the leader lock is stale.
Check replica replication lag before promoting anything.
If automatic promotion has not run and lag is acceptable, promote the replica manually per the documented command.
Confirm application connection strings or the service endpoint now resolve to the new primary.
Escalate to database on-call immediately; do not promote without them on the call for SEV-1.

title: Postgres connection pool saturation
trigger: pgbouncer rejects connections, or pool utilisation stays above 90%.
steps: Read pgbouncer pool utilisation and the waiting client count.
Attribute server connections to client services and note the top consumer.
Check for a recent scale-out: replica count multiplied by per-replica pool size is the real demand.
Check for long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions holding connections.
Cap batch concurrency at the pool size rather than raising the pool to match the batch.
Escalate to database on-call before raising max_connections on the server.

title: Deployment rollback decision and procedure
trigger: A deploy is a candidate cause for an active incident.
steps: Establish the deploy time and the symptom onset time, and state the gap between them explicitly.
Confirm the deploy reached the replicas that are failing; a partial rollout changes the picture.
Read the diff for changes to dependency call patterns, pool sizes, timeouts, and feature flags.
If a feature flag can disable the new path, prefer that over a rollback.
Roll back to the last known good version and record the start and finish times.
Verify recovery against the same metric that triggered the alert before declaring mitigation.
Keep the rollback artefact for the postmortem; do not redeploy the suspect version to reproduce in production.

title: Notification queue backlog
trigger: Queue depth is growing monotonically, or delivery lag exceeds five minutes.
steps: Read queue depth, enqueue rate, and drain rate; a backlog needs the difference, not the depth alone.
Check whether a campaign or batch job is enqueueing above the normal rate.
Check worker error rates before scaling; failing workers do not drain faster when multiplied.
Before scaling out, compute the Postgres and Redis connections the new replica count will hold.
Scale out only within the dependency connection budget. INC-1120 scaled out and INC-1320 had to scale back in for that reason.
Escalate to platform if the backlog persists at the connection budget ceiling.

title: TLS certificate expiry response
trigger: TLS handshake failures between services, or a certificate within 72 hours of expiry.
steps: Read the certificate expiry on the failing endpoint and compare it against the symptom onset minute.
An onset that lands exactly on an expiry timestamp and no deploy nearby points away from a release.
Check whether the service is registered with the rotation automation.
Issue and deploy a replacement certificate through the normal pipeline.
Re-register the service for rotation and confirm the next renewal date.
Escalate to platform if the automation silently skipped the service.

title: Slow query triage
trigger: Latency rises while the error rate stays flat, and the service is database-backed.
steps: Confirm the error rate is flat; latency without errors usually means the work got slower, not that it failed.
Read pg_stat_statements for the queries whose mean time changed most against the previous day.
Run EXPLAIN on the top offender and look for a sequential scan where an index scan is expected.
Check recent migrations for dropped or renamed indexes.
Check autovacuum lag and dead tuple ratio on the hot tables.
Recreate a missing index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; escalate to database on-call for anything that locks.

title: Auth API rate limiting and 429 responses
trigger: auth-api returns HTTP 429 above 1% of requests.
steps: Confirm the responses are 429 and not 5xx; a limiter fault and a service fault need different paths.
Read the effective rate limit value and, critically, its scope. Global versus per-tenant is the usual defect.
Check whether a deploy or config refresh changed the limiter key.
Look for a single tenant driving the traffic before widening the limit for everyone.
Restore the intended scope rather than raising the number.
Escalate to identity if the limiter counter store itself is unreachable.
